summary:
Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156, which carry up to fourteen years' imprisonment, and left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned of heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence against LGBT people.

The application was brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who had received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs in the proceedings, and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming that the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage.

Human Rights Watch reported in October 2018, in the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and at times assaulted them in custody. The report found that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted.

Medical services are refused on gender-expression grounds. The same report documented a trans man who was beaten and then denied treatment, and nurses who mocked people presenting for HIV tests.

Sections 153 and 156 carry up to fourteen years for men and five years for women. A 2012 moratorium on arrests issued by the justice minister was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 following litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium while both provisions faced a constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed his custody.

Arrests have been accompanied by community violence. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 had their house ransacked, were assaulted by neighbours and threatened with being burned alive, and faced attempted extortion and humiliation by community police, including forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photographs distributed on social media.

The United States State Department's 2011 human rights report for Malawi documented discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, harsh prison conditions, and twenty people killed in the protest killings of July 2011.
tangentialFactors:
Religious mobilisation is the principal force shaping the legal environment. Faith-based organisations filed briefs defending the penal provisions, and religious leaders organised nationwide protests in 2023 and litigation in 2016 that produced the suspension of the moratorium on arrests.

Reform now runs only through parliament, which the Constitutional Court expressly designated as the body to consider any change to sections 153, 154 and 156. No legislative movement is sourced in the material.

Prison conditions form part of the risk picture: a trans woman was held for eight years in a men's prison, and a foreign government's 2011 reporting described Malawi's prisons as harsh.

External monitoring continues through foreign government human rights reporting and international human rights organisations, both of which have published detailed findings on Malawi's treatment of LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Residents face up to fourteen years under section 153 for men and five years under section 156 for women. The 2012 moratorium on arrests remains legally contested after the Mzuzu High Court suspended it in 2016, and police have been recorded choosing charges designed to avoid it.

Local organisations work inside these constraints. Gift Trapence of CEDEP contrasted the December 2015 arrests with government spending of Global Fund money on HIV services for LGBTI people, an example of the gap between funded health programming and criminal enforcement.

Human Rights Watch based its 2018 findings on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre, plus lawyers, activists and officials, and reported that police arbitrarily detained transgender people and that medical staff refused or mocked people seeking care.

Community-level enforcement is documented: in the December 2015 arrests, community police carried out forced stripping and forced medical examinations and circulated photographs of the detainees.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition or the rules governing sex and gender markers on passports and identity documents, so that question is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening procedures for trans travellers are not sourced, including whether presentation at immigration raises any risk of refusal or referral.

Whether the moratorium on arrests is currently operative in practice after the June 2024 Constitutional Court ruling is unresolved; the inventory contains no enforcement statistics or arrest data for the period after the judgment.

Hate-crime provisions, facilities and bathroom rules, access to transition-related healthcare, and recognition of partners or marriages beyond the dismissed application are not covered by the available sources.
